design_detail: Naturalistic field study of two self-selected parallel groups followed over five days, without a measurement before the drug night: 12 people who said they had taken ecstasy (MDMA) on a Saturday night at one London club and 12 who said they had drunk alcohol but taken no illicit drug, tested that night in a quiet room in the club while intoxicated (day 1), at home the next afternoon (day 2) and at home on the Wednesday evening (day 5). Measures: Beck Depression Inventory, 16 Bond-Lader mood visual analogue scales, 14 bodily-symptom visual analogue scales, serial sevens and Rivermead prose recall (immediate and delayed). Repeated-measures ANOVA with group (between) and day (within).
can_establish: How self-rated mood, bodily symptoms and two simple cognitive tasks changed over the five days after a Saturday night of self-reported ecstasy use, compared with a Saturday night of heavy drinking, in 24 young adults from one club.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy caused the mid-week changes (no pre-drug measurement, intake not verified, self-selected groups that differed in other drug use, unblinded assessor, testing time and place changing with the day), how many people developed low mood (no individual counts above any cut-off are given), or anything about known doses of pure MDMA.

sample.recruitment: Club setting on successive Saturday nights over four months, snowball technique (p. 823). The assessing psychologist had previously worked as a part-time disc jockey at the club, which made testing there possible (p. 822).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Volunteers who reported taking only MDMA or only alcohol (apart from caffeine or nicotine) on the night; people reporting other drugs, or a combination of MDMA and alcohol, were not included (p. 823). Ages 20 to 27.
sample.demographics: Eight men and four women in each group; ecstasy group six degree students and six employed, alcohol group seven students and five employed (p. 823).
sample.attrition: None: all 24 were tested on all three occasions and re-consented on day 2 (p. 823).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected club-goers willing to be tested in a club and at home; snowball recruitment; groups formed by what people said they took that night. The ecstasy group reported more regular use of several drugs (alcohol, cannabis, MDMA, cocaine); 7 of the 12 in the alcohol group had also used MDMA (3 about monthly, 4 occasionally) (p. 824). The authors had no drug-free volunteers in that setting (p. 822).

exposure.measurement: Self-report on day 2 of what had been taken the previous night; no blood, urine or tablet testing (pp. 824, 829). The authors argue that the acute mood profile matched earlier studies of pure MDMA (p. 829).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: tablets sold as ecstasy, number and content not recorded; 7 of the 12 in the ecstasy group also drank 1 to 3 units of alcohol (mean 1.8), mostly before arriving; the alcohol group drank 4 to 14 units (mean 10.8) (p. 824). Usual frequency in the ecstasy group: 2 about weekly, 6 about monthly, 4 occasionally (p. 824).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol on the night in 7 of 12 in the ecstasy group (acknowledged as a limitation, p. 829); lifetime use of cannabis, cocaine and other drugs higher in the ecstasy group, not quantified or adjusted. Participants were asked not to drink or use illicit drugs between testings; one person drank 3 units between days 2 and 5 and none reported illicit drugs (p. 824); not verified.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Day 1 was measured during intoxication in both groups; days 2 and 5 after self-reported abstinence, unverified.

comparison.controls: 12 club-goers who reported drinking alcohol but no illicit drug that night.
comparison.matching: Same sex split and similar ages and occupations; no formal matching or adjustment.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure of mood, sleep, cognition, psychiatric history or life events before the drug night; usual mood is unknown in both groups.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The alcohol group drank about ten times as much that night and was itself hung over on day 2 (the authors read its U-shaped course as a hangover, p. 826); most of its members had used MDMA before.

outcomes.instruments: Beck Depression Inventory at each testing point; 16 Bond-Lader mood visual analogue scales (100 mm); 14 bodily-symptom visual analogue scales; serial sevens (correct subtractions and errors in 120 seconds); Rivermead prose recall, immediate and delayed, three versions balanced across people and days (pp. 823-824).
outcomes.validity_norms: The paper cites BDI scores below 9 as normal and above 16 as indicating clinical depression (p. 825); the visual analogue scales have no norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Low mood was read from BDI totals and mood ratings; no diagnostic interview. A reanalysis dropping the BDI's sleep and appetite items was reported (p. 829).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Editors' count from Tables 1 to 3: 4 cognitive scores, the BDI, 16 mood scales and 14 bodily scales, each with group, day and interaction tests; the authors mention 34 variables and that 1.7 results would be significant at 0.05 by chance (p. 826).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: one psychologist recruited and tested everyone and knew who had taken what.

analysis.effect_sizes: The paper gives only significance levels (stars or p thresholds) for group, day and group x day effects, with no F values, degrees of freedom, effect sizes or simple-effect tests. BDI means (SD) on days 1, 2 and 5: ecstasy 3.5 (3.5), 8.7 (3.8), 11.8 (7.2); alcohol 6.4 (5.3), 8.3 (5.2), 6.9 (4.1); group x day p<0.001, group not significant (Table 2, p. 827). Editors' calculation from these means and SDs (independent t-test, 12 per group): the day-5 difference is 4.9 points, 95% CI -0.1 to 9.9, t(22) = 2.05, p = 0.053, d = 0.84; on day 2 the groups do not differ (8.7 against 8.3). Serial sevens: group p<0.01, group x day p<0.05 (pp. 824-825).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable for a 1996 field study; no protocol mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 35 measures are tabulated (Tables 1 to 3), but only with significance marks; no exact statistics or individual counts above BDI cut-offs.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 12 per group. The authors say a delayed-recall difference might have reached significance with a larger sample (p. 829).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The ecstasy group felt elevated on the night and its mood ratings then fell across the next days, while the alcohol group dipped on day 2 and recovered. On day 2 both groups were similar on the BDI (8.7 against 8.3) and many mood scales; the ecstasy group was markedly more tired and lacking in energy. By the Wednesday the ecstasy group's mean BDI was 11.8 against 6.9, with higher ratings of sadness, depression, anxiety, agitation and irritability; the day-5 BDI difference taken alone is borderline (editors' calculation p = 0.053) and the interaction is partly driven by the ecstasy group's low score while intoxicated on day 1. The ecstasy group made fewer correct subtractions on all three days.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says some participants scored within the range for clinical depression on day 5 and that weekend MDMA use may lead to depressed mood mid-week (p. 821); the Results say some were in the mild to moderate range (p. 825) without a count, and the day-5 group mean lies between the normal and clinical cut-offs the paper cites. The abstract presents the serial-sevens result as an impairment from MDMA, although the ecstasy group was lower on every day, including mid-week, so a pre-existing difference cannot be excluded without a baseline. The discussion is open about the field design's limits (pp. 829-830) and offers three explanations (temporary serotonin depletion, neurotoxicity, a psychological reaction to the high) without testing any.

timeline.event: This study: first field report of a mid-week low after weekend ecstasy use, against people who had been drinking.

Scott et al.: people who used ecstasy at the weekend did not differ from people who use ecstasy but abstained that week on distress, mood or clinician ratings one and three days later, against each person's own baseline.

replication.where_it_stands: A small, early, influential field study. A later study with a pre-use baseline and an ecstasy-using comparison group did not find a group difference (Scott et al., 2013). Parrott and Lasky (1998; card sc_parrott_1998) also measured mood two and seven days after a Saturday night and should be read together with these two.

funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, University College London. The second author, who did the testing, had worked as a part-time disc jockey at the club where everyone was recruited (p. 822).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people who already use ecstasy that measures mood and sleep before a planned weekend of use and daily for a week afterwards, against people from the same scene who go out, dance and stay up without taking ecstasy, with tablet testing or urine confirmation, blinded assessment, objective sleep measures and counts of how many people cross a depression cut-off.

domains.note: No measurement before the drug night; the groups differed in lifetime drug use and in how much alcohol they drank that night, and sleep loss and dancing were not measured; nothing was adjusted.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Self-reported intake, tablets of unknown content, and 7 of 12 in the ecstasy group also drank.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Snowball recruitment of volunteers at one club, grouped by what they chose to take that night.
Abstinence between testings was requested but not checked; sleep between testings not recorded.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Self-rated scales collected by an assessor who knew the groups; setting and time of day changed with the day (club at night, home at midday, home in the evening), and practice effects were large.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: 35 measures without correction, results reported only as significance marks, and no simple-effect test for the mid-week day.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The study can be cited for the pattern of self-rated mood and tiredness over five days in these 24 people, and for the contrast with a group recovering from heavy drinking. It cannot be cited as showing that ecstasy causes low mood mid-week: there is no pre-drug baseline, the comparison group differs in what it drank and in drug history, intake was not verified and the assessor was not blind. Very high risk of bias for any causal reading.

key_findings.finding: Beck Depression Inventory, means (SD) on days 1, 2 and 5: ecstasy group 3.5 (3.5), 8.7 (3.8), 11.8 (7.2); alcohol group 6.4 (5.3), 8.3 (5.2), 6.9 (4.1). Group not significant, day p<0.001, group x day p<0.001. The text gives the ecstasy day-5 mean as 11.75 and says the spread was larger on day 5, with some people in the normal range and others in the mild to moderate depression range; no count is given.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, BDI row (p. 827); Results, Beck Depression Inventory paragraph (p. 825, left column); Fig. 2 (p. 826)

key_findings.finding: With the BDI's somatic items (sleep, appetite) removed, the pattern and the group x day interaction (p<0.001) remained: ecstasy 2.25, 6.91, 9.92 and alcohol 5.08, 6.83, 5.49 on days 1, 2 and 5.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 826, the reanalysis on p. 829, left column)

key_findings.finding: Mood scales (0-100 mm): 11 of 16 showed group x day interactions; the strongest (p<0.001) were contented-discontented, happy-sad and interested-bored. Sad: ecstasy 7.0 (9.9), 33.5 (20.7), 54.6 (27.7); alcohol 26.9 (21.8), 41.6 (18.5), 35.1 (16.9). Bored: ecstasy 14.4, 49.6, 62.8; alcohol 41.9, 55.9, 39.4. On day 2 the two groups were broadly similar; the authors liken the ecstasy day after to an alcohol hangover in some respects.
key_findings.locator: Results, Mood rating scale paragraphs (p. 825, right column); Table 2 (p. 827); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 826)

key_findings.finding: Bodily symptoms (0-100 mm), days 1, 2 and 5. Lack of energy: ecstasy 10.6 (9.7), 82.2 (11.4), 68.6 (15.1); alcohol 38.8 (22.5), 65.8 (8.5), 48.7 (23.8). Physical tiredness: ecstasy 15.1, 78.9 (11.7), 60.0; alcohol 41.9, 64.5 (5.9), 46.1. Both group x day p<0.001. Headache rose on day 2 in both groups (ecstasy 58.3, alcohol 50.2; interaction not significant).
key_findings.locator: Results, Bodily Symptoms Scale paragraph (p. 826, left column); Table 3 (p. 828)

key_findings.finding: Day 5 bodily ratings, ecstasy against alcohol group: depression 56.3 (24.4) against 20.7 (13.6); anxiety 52.2 (21.2) against 26.9 (18.7); agitation 60.8 (21.1) against 24.5 (15.4); irritability 63.6 (17.6) against 44.1 (18.3). Group x day interactions p<0.01 for depression, anxiety and agitation and p<0.05 for irritability; in the ecstasy group these rose progressively over the days.
key_findings.locator: Results, Bodily Symptoms Scale paragraph (p. 826); Table 3 (p. 828)

key_findings.finding: Serial sevens, correct subtractions in 120 s, means (SD) days 1, 2, 5: ecstasy 2.7 (1.9), 14.2 (6.7), 25.1 (7.1); alcohol 6.3 (3.4), 26.6 (10.7), 31.1 (11.1). Group p<0.01, day p<0.001, group x day p<0.05; the ecstasy group made fewer subtractions at every point, most clearly on day 2; errors did not differ. Prose recall showed only a trend for lower scores in the ecstasy group (p<0.06) and improvement over days in both groups.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 824); Results, Prose recall and Serial sevens paragraphs (pp. 824-825); Fig. 1 (p. 825)

key_findings.finding: Alcohol on the night: 7 of the 12 in the ecstasy group also drank, far less than the alcohol group (amounts in the exposure field); one person drank between days 2 and 5.
key_findings.locator: Results, Participants' reported drug use, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Most of the ecstasy group reported lack of sleep on day 2; the authors cannot say whether the day-2 subtraction deficit was a drug effect or due to lost sleep. Sleep was not measured.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph continuing from p. 829 (p. 830, left column, top)

key_findings.finding: Testing times: day 1 in the club at night; day 2 at home between 12:00 and 16:00; day 5 at home between about 17:30 and 20:30.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion rule excluded anyone who had combined MDMA and alcohol (p. 823), but 7 of the 12 in the ecstasy group reported drinking 1 to 3 units that night (p. 824).
reporting_issues.consequence: The ecstasy group is an ecstasy-plus-some-alcohol group; the authors acknowledge this as a limitation (p. 829).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says two bodily-symptom scales had group x day interactions at the 0.05 level (p. 826), but Table 3 marks three at p<0.05 (irritability, impaired concentration, dry mouth) (p. 828).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table is the record to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says some participants scored within the range for clinical depression (p. 821); the Results say mild to moderate range (p. 825); no number of people above either cut-off is reported anywhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper cannot be cited for how many people had depressed mood; only the group means can be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors mention 34 variables (p. 826) while Tables 1 to 3 hold 35 measures (editors' count); none of the tests is reported with a statistic or degrees of freedom.
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes and simple effects cannot be checked from the paper; the editors' day-5 calculation from the printed means and SDs is borderline (p = 0.053).

reporting_issues.issue: The PDF is a scanned copy with an optical-character text layer; Tables 2 and 3 are printed sideways and their text layer is unreadable, so all values were read from rendered page images.
reporting_issues.consequence: A second reader should check the table values against the page images, not the text layer.
